lead: A pacemaker is a small implanted generator that gives a timed electrical pulse to the heart when the heart's own conduction fails. The pulse starts a contraction; the muscle does the pumping. A defibrillator gives one large shock to stop chaotic fibrillation, so a normal rhythm can restart. Pacemakers run for years on a lithium-iodine cell. Defibrillators store energy in a capacitor and release it through paddles or implanted leads. Both are used in emergency care, cardiology wards and implanted therapy.
prereq: You need resting and action potentials and ECG recording, and arrhythmia monitoring. The circuit that keeps the ECG monitor alive during a shock is covered with defibrillator protection and cardiac ablation.

blocks.text: An internal pacemaker is implanted under the skin, usually below the collarbone. A lead runs through a vein to the right ventricle; its tip electrode touches the heart muscle. An external pacemaker does the same job from outside the body. In an emergency it paces through large skin pads on the chest; because the current must cross the chest wall it needs about 40–200 mA in pulses of 20–40 ms, far more than an implanted lead, and the chest muscles twitch. After heart surgery a temporary external box drives a wire passed through a vein or sewn onto the heart. The generator has a cell, a timing circuit, an output stage and a sense amplifier.

The lead may be unipolar or bipolar. In unipolar pacing, current flows from the tip electrode to the metal case of the generator, so the path is long. In bipolar pacing, current flows between two close electrodes on the lead tip; the path is short, so it is less affected by muscle noise. Bipolar leads are common today.

Fixed-rate mode fires at a set rate, for example 70 pulses per minute (ppm), whatever the heart does. Demand mode, also called R-wave inhibited, listens for the heart's own QRS complex. If a beat is sensed within the timing window, the output is inhibited; if no beat appears, the pacemaker fires. This avoids competition with the heart's own rhythm.

The output stage charges a small capacitor from the cell between beats and empties it into the lead through a coupling capacitor, so each pulse is a short rectangle of about 2.5–5 V (programmable), a few milliamperes into a lead impedance of about 500 Ω. The coupling capacitor blocks any steady current, which would corrode the electrode and injure the tissue at the tip. A three-letter code names the type: chamber paced, chamber sensed, response to a sensed beat. VOO is fixed-rate ventricular pacing, VVI is ventricular demand pacing and DDD paces and senses both atrium and ventricle.

Batteries. The lithium-iodine cell has been the standard since the 1970s: about 2.8 V, 1–2.5 Ah, very low self-discharge and a slow, predictable voltage fall near the end of life, so the pacemaker signals that replacement is due months ahead. Earlier implants used mercury-zinc cells (1.35 V each), which lasted only about 2–3 years and released hydrogen gas; a few used nuclear cells heated by plutonium-238, and rechargeable nickel-cadmium cells were tried and dropped. External pacemakers use ordinary replaceable batteries, such as a 9 V cell, because the box stays outside the body.

items: Pacing rate is counted in pulses per minute; 60 ppm means one pulse every 1 s.
Pulse width is the duration of each pulse, usually 0.5–2 ms. A short pulse excites the muscle and keeps average current low.
A lithium-iodine cell gives about 2.8 V and a capacity in ampere-hours (Ah).

blocks.where: Q<sub>batt</sub> is cell capacity in Ah, I<sub>avg</sub> is average current in A, and 8760 is hours per year.

blocks.text: Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic electrical activity; the heart quivers and does not pump. A defibrillator charges a capacitor and discharges it through the chest or implanted leads for a few milliseconds. This large current stuns the heart muscle, so all cells recover together and a normal rhythm can restart.

An AC defibrillator applied mains current from a step-up transformer, about 250–750 V at 50 Hz for 0.25–1 s, across the heart. It needed mains power, damaged more muscle and could not be made portable, so the DC defibrillator replaced it. A DC defibrillator charges a capacitor and then empties it in one short pulse. External units use paddles or adhesive pads on the chest, one below the right collarbone beside the sternum and one over the apex, or one in front and one on the back. Internal defibrillation uses small paddles placed directly on the heart during open-chest surgery, at about 5–50 J, and an implanted cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) shocks through its own leads at up to about 35–40 J.

The DC defibrillator circuit. A step-up transformer, or a DC-to-DC converter in a battery unit, raises the voltage; a rectifier and a current-limiting resistor charge the storage capacitor, typically 16–32 µF, to as much as 5 kV. A high-voltage charge–discharge switch first connects the capacitor to the charger and then, when both paddle buttons are pressed, to the patient. In the classic Lown circuit a series inductor of about 50–100 mH shapes the discharge into a damped half-sine pulse about 5 ms long instead of a sharp spike. The stored energy is shared between the chest, about 50 Ω, and the internal resistance of the inductor, switch and cables, so the delivered energy is less than the stored energy. Biphasic units reverse the current partway with a bridge of electronic switches and adjust the pulse to the measured chest impedance.

Waveforms are monophasic or biphasic. Monophasic sends current in one direction; external settings go up to 360 J. Biphasic reverses current partway through; a typical external setting is 200 J. Biphasic is common because it often defibrillates at lower energy.

Unsynchronised defibrillation fires at once, for ventricular fibrillation. Synchronised cardioversion times the shock to the R wave, for rhythms such as atrial fibrillation; it avoids firing in the vulnerable T wave. The protection circuit that saves the ECG amplifier from this shock is in defibrillator protection and cardiac ablation.

blocks.where: E is stored energy in joules, C is capacitance in farads, and V is capacitor voltage in volts. Charge is Q = C V, in coulombs.

figure.caption: The worked example's defibrillator: the charger fills a 32 µF capacitor to 5000 V (400 J, 0.16 C); the switch then empties it through the inductor and 10 Ω of internal resistance into a 50 Ω chest, which receives 333 J as a damped half-sine pulse about 5 ms long.

spec.aria: Circuit of a DC defibrillator: charger and charging resistor feed a 32 microfarad capacitor at 5000 volts; a discharge switch connects it through a 50 millihenry inductor and a 10 ohm internal resistance to a 50 ohm chest. A sum box gives 400 joules stored and 333 joules delivered, and a small graph shows the damped half-sine current pulse of about 5 milliseconds.

examples.question: A DC defibrillator charges a 32 µF capacitor to 5000 V. Find the energy stored and the charge on the capacitor.
steps: Given C = 32 µF = 32×10⁻⁶ F and V = 5000 V.
Stored energy E = ½ C V² = 0.5 × 32×10⁻⁶ F × (5000 V)².
Charge Q = C V = 32×10⁻⁶ F × 5000 V = 0.16 C.

Not all of it reaches the patient. The capacitor discharges through the internal resistance of the inductor, switch and cables in series with the chest. With 10 Ω inside the machine and 50 Ω of chest, the patient receives 50 ÷ (50 + 10) = 0.83 of the energy: 0.83 × 400 J = 333 J. The other 67 J heats the internal resistance.
examples.answer: Energy stored = 400 J; charge on the capacitor = 0.16 C; with 10 Ω of internal resistance about 333 J reaches a 50 Ω chest.

examples.question: An implanted pacemaker paces at 70 ppm with pulses of 2.5 V and 0.5 ms into a lead impedance of 500 Ω. Its sensing and timing circuits draw a steady 10 µA. The lithium-iodine cell has a usable capacity of 1.2 Ah. Find the pulse current, the charge per pulse, the average current and the battery life in years.
steps: Pulse current I = V ÷ R = 2.5 V ÷ 500 Ω = 5 mA.
Charge per pulse q = I × t = 5 × 10⁻³ A × 0.5 × 10⁻³ s = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ C = 2.5 µC.
Pulses per second = 70 ÷ 60 = 1.167, so the pacing current averages 2.5 µC × 1.167 per second = 2.92 µA.
Total average current I<sub>avg</sub> = 2.92 µA + 10 µA = 12.92 µA.
Charge used per year = 12.92 × 10⁻⁶ A × 8760 h = 0.1132 Ah.
Life = 1.2 Ah ÷ 0.1132 Ah per year = 10.6 years. The steady circuit drain uses more charge than the pulses themselves.
examples.answer: Pulse current 5 mA, 2.5 µC per pulse, average current about 12.9 µA and a battery life of about 10.6 years.

traps: Do not mix energy, charge and voltage: E = ½CV² gives joules, Q = CV gives coulombs, V is volts. The capacitance must be in farads, not microfarads.
A pacemaker does not pump blood. It only triggers a contraction; the heart muscle does the pumping.
Unsynchronised defibrillation is not synchronised cardioversion. Cardioversion times the shock to the R wave; defibrillation fires immediately.
Fixed-rate pacing fires at the set rate regardless of intrinsic beats; demand mode inhibits when a beat is sensed.
External defibrillation uses more energy than internal defibrillation because the current path is longer and loss is greater.

quiz.q: Which cell is used in an implanted pacemaker and what is its nominal voltage?
Why does demand mode inhibit the pacemaker output?
quiz.a: It senses the heart's own QRS; if a beat is present, firing is not needed and is stopped to avoid competition.

quiz.q: A pacemaker cell has 2.0 Ah capacity and average current 10 µA. Find life in years.
quiz.a: I = 10 µA = 10×10⁻⁶ A. Life = 2.0 / (10×10⁻⁶ × 8760) = 22.8 years. That is the ideal figure; real pacemakers last about 7–12 years, because part of the capacity cannot be used near the end of life and the output settings and pacing rate vary.

quiz.q: Why is less energy needed for internal defibrillation than external defibrillation?
quiz.a: Electrodes are close to the heart, so the current path is short and fewer losses occur; less energy reaches threshold.

quiz.q: A 50 µF capacitor is charged to 4000 V. Find stored energy.
State one difference between monophasic and biphasic defibrillation.
quiz.a: Monophasic current flows one way; biphasic reverses direction partway. Biphasic often uses lower energy.

quiz.q: Why is pacemaker pulse width only 0.5–2 ms?
quiz.a: A short pulse excites cardiac muscle and keeps average current and battery drain low; a long pulse wastes charge.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern work includes leadless pacemakers, MRI-conditional leads and subcutaneous ICDs. Wearable defibrillators monitor and shock outside hospital. Research looks at better biphasic waveforms and smaller batteries. Search for leadless pacemaker, subcutaneous ICD and biphasic defibrillation waveform.
